parsed.explanation: The combined regime is sharply split. State level is among the most protective documented: a shield law blocking other jurisdictions' care-related warrants and custody orders, gender-identity anti-discrimination law since 1993, hate-crime coverage, X licences, protected care access, repealed sodomy law, trans-panic ban, no local facility ban. But the national layer faces every traveller at entry: binary sex-marker passports, a 2025 visa cable directing officers to refuse cases on document or sex discrepancy and to weigh permanent fraud findings, foreign-government advisories after detentions, plus documented national custody harms (hormone removal, forced labour, sexual abuse of trans detainees) and state-endorsed threat-framing of trans people. Universal border/document exposure with no working national remedy, inside a genuinely protective local layer, lands in elevated risk near the higher edge.

entry_documents.exposure: National passports/visas restricted to birth-sex markers; X processing stopped; 2025 cable orders refusal on document/sex discrepancy and weighs lifetime fraud ineligibility; reported passport confiscations stranding travellers; allied states issued trans travel advisories after visa detentions.
entry_documents.protection: Civil-liberties litigation challenging the passport policy is pending; X passports issued before policy remain valid until expiry.
entry_documents.interaction: Entry is national law; the protective state cannot alter visa adjudication or screening at national ports.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: National corrections bureau adopted birth-sex-linked policies from 2026 including hormone removal; trans men in immigration custody reported forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse; reporting ceased on trans prisoner numbers.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: State shield law bars enforcement of out-of-state warrants over lawful care; state corrections placement documented only for a 2012 case (male facility, assault, later hormone relief).
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A traveller entering any national custody path — visa investigation, immigration detention — faces national rules the state cannot override.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National order bars trans access to congruent government-funded single-sex facilities nationwide; ~21 state/provinces have birth-sex facility bans, 4 with criminal offences; the national sports-ban order and cable create entry refusals.
federal_state_facilities.protection: This state/province is documented in the most-protective tier with no local facility ban in the mapped categories; its anti-discrimination law covers public accommodations.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: National facilities (airports, national buildings) operate under the parent ban; state facilities under protective state law.

care_services.exposure: National hostility to care (orders, funding freezes, hospital record subpoenas) and 27 state/provinces with minor-care bans elsewhere; adult-with-minor travellers entering other state/provinces face those bans.
care_services.protection: Shield law prevents enforcement of other jurisdictions' care-related subpoenas, warrants, extraditions and custody removals; insurers cannot exclude trans care; public insurance covers it; conversion therapy banned.
care_services.interaction: A travelling family seeking care here is protected locally; national insurance rules and federal scrutiny are not displaced.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National orders frame trans identity as deception ('chemical and surgical mutilation', fraud framing at visa stage); counterterrorism strategy names 'radically pro-transgender' groups for prioritisation; violent rhetoric exists in many state/provinces.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: State law abolished the trans panic defence and criminalises conversion therapy; state officials frame care as legitimate.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: National framing shapes visa officers and national law enforcement whom the traveller first encounters; state framing shapes daily life inside the state.

minors_guardians.exposure: A travelling minor's social transition is criminal-prosecution exposure under the January 2025 national order in national-scope scenarios; out-of-state custody-removal orders over care obtained here are a risk elsewhere.
minors_guardians.protection: Shield law blocks removal of children for care obtained here; state bans conversion therapy; state athlete policy contested in court, outcome unknown.
minors_guardians.interaction: State protection is strong but sits against a national order authorising prosecution of facilitators — the harshest operative rule governs any national interaction.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: Bias violence exists (orientation-based incidents a consistent share of hate crime); 37 state/provinces lacked GI bias statutes in 2019; one state arrest under a bathroom law (handcuffed, 24 hours in a men's ward) shows enforcement elsewhere.
street_violence_police_response.protection: State hate-crime law covers gender identity since 1993; anti-discrimination law is long-standing; enforcement data for outcomes not sourced here.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: Inside this state, police response is governed by state statutes; recourse quality is documented as law but not as outcome data.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No state enforcement/complaint outcome data for discrimination or hate-crime provisions; shield law applied in no sourced decided case; custody placement present-day practice undocumented; athlete-policy challenge unresolved.
remedies_unknowns.protection: Judicial challenges to national passport and care rules remain live; protections could expand if litigation succeeds.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: Unresolved questions lighten but do not erase exposures; the operative national rules at entry are currently in effect.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar: a universal national-level exposure (here, entry/document regime with discrepancy refusals and fraud findings) coexisting with documented protective elements and no local offence. Here the local layer is far stronger (shield law, 30+ years of anti-discrimination law), but national custody harms and entry refusals are more severe than Melavi's single ward directive, keeping it nearby rather than above.

This case exceeds Teravi in one direction: its national layer is more hostile (organised custody abuse, counterterrorism framing, allied travel advisories) than ferry-operator rudeness; but its local protections are far more institutionalised. Net position sits at the upper edge of elevated risk rather than clearly in reduced risk.

Ilvora has a dead-letter tangential statute and otherwise no operative restriction. Here the national restrictions are live and enforced at the border — passports, visa cable, screening — so despite comparable local acceptance and protections, this case must sit materially below Ilvora.

parsed.synthesis: The operative regime is two-layered. Inside the state, a traveller finds the strongest documented protective stack in the dossier: care shield, identity-based anti-discrimination and hate-crime law, X markers, care coverage, no local facility or presentation offence. Every traveller, however, passes first through a national gate that is currently hostile: binary-only markers, refusals on discrepancy, potential lifetime fraud findings, national facility bans, and documented custody harms including medication denial and sexual abuse in national detention. The harshest operative rule governs the moments of highest consequence — entry, adjudication, any detention — while the protective state governs everyday life after clearing the gate. That combination — tier-1-scale universal entry exposure with no national remedy, buffered by genuinely operating local protections and no local targeting — places the jurisdiction in elevated risk at the upper end, roughly 0.57.
